messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 57
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Physical Therapist
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 39

She is 57, a physical therapist who has spent most of her adult life teaching other people how to trust their bodies again. In the clinic, she is steady and practical. She shows patients how to shift weight after surgery, how to breathe through pain, how to take one more step than they think they can. Her coworkers know her as calm under pressure. That steadiness is part of how she survived the earthquake eight years ago, and part of how no one fully sees what it still costs her.

At the time, she is living in a coastal city in Latin America with her husband and her younger sister nearby. The morning of the earthquake begins ordinarily. She is getting ready for work, thinking about a patient recovering from a hip fracture, irritated that she cannot find one of her shoes. Then the floor gives a strange, rolling movement beneath her, so unfamiliar at first that she thinks she is dizzy. A second later the walls begin to groan. Glass breaks somewhere in the apartment. The lights go out.

She runs toward the hallway, shouting for her husband. The building is shaking so hard she cannot stay upright. She drops to her knees and crawls, feeling the tiles buck under her palms. She remembers the sound more than anything else—the concrete grinding, car alarms outside, people screaming from other apartments. She reaches the doorway just as a shelf crashes behind her. For a moment she is certain the building is going to fold in on itself.

She and her husband make it outside with dozens of neighbors, some barefoot, some bleeding. The street is split in places. Power lines sag low. Dust hangs in the air so thick she tastes it. Her sister does not answer her phone. For hours she cannot locate her. She moves automatically, the way she does in emergencies at work, helping an older man sit down, wrapping a towel around a child’s cut foot, counting people, scanning faces. Inside, though, she feels a rising terror she cannot organize. Each aftershock sends her body into immediate panic. Even after she finds her sister alive by evening, she cannot stop shaking.

In the weeks that follow, she sleeps in fragments. She keeps her clothes on at night in case she has to run. When trucks pass outside, the vibration jolts her upright before she is fully awake. She begins mapping exits everywhere she goes: at the grocery store, at church, in restaurants, in her own clinic. She avoids elevators and refuses to enter older buildings alone. When patients mention back pain from “the stress of the quake,” she smiles tightly and changes the subject.

She returns to work quickly because routine feels safer than sitting still. Yet the clinic becomes full of reminders. If a heavy therapy ball drops, her heart races and her hands go cold. When she is guiding a patient on the parallel bars and feels a tremor—sometimes real, sometimes only a truck outside—she loses track of what she is saying. She becomes embarrassed by how often she startles. Once, during a power outage at work, she has to lock herself in the supply room because she is suddenly back in her apartment hallway, on her knees, waiting for concrete to fall. Afterward she tells a coworker she had a migraine.

Her marriage, already strained, thins further in the years after the disaster. Her husband wants life to return to normal and grows impatient with her precautions, her insistence on discussing emergency kits, her refusal to vacation anywhere with high-rise hotels. She experiences him as dismissive and begins keeping more to herself. Their divorce comes later and for many reasons, but she thinks the earthquake changed the emotional language of the marriage. It made her feel alone in a way she had not felt before.

Now, years later, she still measures every room for safety without meaning to. She says she is “always a little on guard.” She avoids the waterfront district where several buildings collapsed, even though it adds twenty minutes to her commute. During seismic reports on the news, she cannot look away, then feels foolish for sitting with her shoes on, pulse pounding, as if she might need to flee. At night she sometimes dreams that she is searching for her sister through clouds of dust, unable to shout loudly enough. She wakes with her jaw clenched and her chest tight, already listening for movement in the walls.

What troubles her most is how her body no longer feels fully trustworthy to her. As a physical therapist, she has spent decades believing that with practice and patience the body can relearn safety. But when the ground seems to shift beneath her—even for an instant—her body answers before thought. Her shoulders tense, her breath turns shallow, and she is no longer a skilled clinician in sensible shoes. She is a woman in a dark hallway, crawling toward a door, trying to get out before everything comes down.
